title: Importing data into RStudio with R
text:
1. Set up an RStudio Project
Start every analysis in an RStudio Project (File → New Project). A project sets the working directory to the project folder, so file paths are the same on every computer that opens it.
A simple layout:
my-analysis/
├── my-analysis.Rproj
├── data/
│   ├── bal_metadata.xlsx
│   ├── bal_cell_counts.xlsx
│   └── bal_baseline.csv
└── analysis.qmd
Put the three downloaded files in data/, then load the packages used in this tutorial (install any you’re missing with install.packages()):

library(readr)    # fast, consistent CSV reading
library(readxl)   # Excel files (.xls and .xlsx)
library(dplyr)    # data manipulation
library(purrr)    # repeat a step over many sheets
library(janitor)  # tidy column names, find duplicates
library(here)     # build file paths from the project root
library(ggplot2)  # a quick plot to check the data

here() builds a path starting from the project root, wherever your script lives:

# In your own project:
metadata_path <- here("data", "bal_metadata.xlsx")







Tip



Avoid setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/..."). A hard-coded path only works on your own computer, and breaks as soon as you move the folder or share it.

title: Importing data into RStudio with R
text:
2. Read a CSV file
bal_baseline.csv is the tidy baseline table. R can read it in two ways.
Base R comes with read.csv():

baseline_base <- read.csv(baseline_path)
str(baseline_base[, 1:6])

 $ pt_id       : chr  "SP34696" "SP22845" "SP31186" "SP39161" ...

 $ tb_diagnosis: chr  "LTBI" "Control" "LTBI" "Control" ...
 $ hiv_status  : chr  "Negative" "Positive" "Negative" "Positive" ...
 $ age_at_visit: int  53 30 15 50 30 35 54 38 20 43 ...
 $ bronc_date  : chr  "2018-07-01" "2020-04-16" "2020-07-01" "2016-07-29" ...

Two things stand out:

The column names contain brackets and slashes (Height_1(cm), IGRA_Value(IU/ml)), so you’d have to wrap them in backticks every time you use them.
Height, weight and IGRA value should be numbers, but they were read as text (<chr>).

Why are they text? Look at the values that aren’t numbers:

metadata_raw |>
  filter(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Height_1(cm)`))),
         !is.na(`Height_1(cm)`)) |>
  count(`Height_1(cm)`, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  `Height_1(cm)`     n
  <chr>          <int>
1 -                  4
2 .                  4
3 N/A                3
4 ND                 3
5 not done           3


The people who entered the data recorded “missing” in five different ways. One text value is enough to make the whole column text. Tell read_excel() which codes mean missing with the na argument, and use clean_names() to fix the column names:

missing_codes <- c("", "N/A", "ND", ".", "-", "not done")

read_excel(metadata_path, sheet = "MetaData", na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names() |>
  select(pt_id, age, height_1_cm, weight_1_kg, igra_value_iu_ml) |>
  glimpse()

Rows: 502
Columns: 5
$ pt_id            <chr> "SP34696", "SP22845", "SP31186", "SP39161", "SP06180"…
$ age              <dbl> 53, 30, 15, 50, 30, 35, 54, 38, 20, 43, 44, 27, 24, 4…
$ height_1_cm      <chr> "182.6", "160.3", "143.9", "165.8", "173.8", "172", "…
$ weight_1_kg      <chr> "55.1", "50.3", "57.7", "59.2", "80.5", "72.099999999…

The column names are fixed and igra_value_iu_ml is now numeric, but height and weight are still text. This is a second, very common Excel problem: numbers stored as text. The cells look like numbers, but Excel saved them as text, and read_excel() keeps whatever type Excel stored.
The reliable fix is to read the sheet as text, then let readr::type_convert() guess each column’s type from its contents, treating the missing-value codes as NA:

metadata <- read_excel(metadata_path, sheet = "MetaData", col_types = "text") |>
  type_convert(na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names()

metadata |>
  select(pt_id, age, height_1_cm, weight_1_kg, igra_value_iu_ml) |>
  glimpse()

All the measurement columns are now numeric (<dbl>), and every column name is lowercase with underscores.






TipOther useful read_excel() arguments




skip = 3 ignores title rows above the table
range = "A1:F200" reads only part of a sheet
col_types = "text" reads everything as text, which is useful when you want to clean values yourself before converting them

5. Check what you imported
Always check a new import before you analyse it. These checks take seconds and catch most problems early.
Categories with inconsistent spelling. count() shows every distinct value:

metadata |>
  count(hiv_status, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  hiv_status     n
  <chr>      <int>
1 Negative     265
2 Positive     170
3 Neg           13
4 POSITIVE      13
5 Pos           12
6 NEGATIVE      11
7 negative      10
8 positive       8


Eight spellings of two answers. Cleaning these up is the next step after importing, but count() is how you find them.
Duplicate participants. Each participant should appear once:

metadata |>
  get_dupes(pt_id) |>
  select(pt_id, dupe_count, sex, age, tb_diagnosis)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  pt_id   dupe_count sex      age tb_diagnosis
  <chr>        <int> <chr>  <dbl> <chr>       
1 SP09573          2 Female    49 Active TB   
2 SP09573          2 Female    49 Active TB   
3 SP22251          2 Male      55 Active TB   
4 SP22251          2 Male      55 Active TB   


Two participants were entered twice. Decide whether to keep the first row or investigate before you join this table to anything else, or the duplicates will multiply your rows.
Missing values per column:

metadata |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(n_missing))

ggplot(metadata, aes(age, fill = tb_diagnosis)) +

title: Importing data into RStudio with R
text:
6. The “Import Dataset” button
RStudio can also import files without writing code: in the Environment pane, choose Import Dataset → From Excel… (or From Text (readr)… for CSV files). The dialog:

Lets you browse to the file and previews the first rows.
Lets you choose the sheet, rows to skip, missing-value codes and column types.
Shows the matching R code in the Code Preview box.

Use the dialog to explore, then copy the code from Code Preview into your script. Imports done only through the dialog aren’t saved anywhere, so nobody (including you, later) can rerun them.

text:
Common pitfalls








Problem
Symptom
Fix




Hard-coded paths
cannot open file 'C:/Users/...' on another computer
Use an RStudio Project and here()


Missing-value codes
Numeric columns read as <chr>
Pass every code to na =


Numbers stored as text in Excel
Still <chr> after setting na; sheets won’t stack
col_types = "text", then type_convert()


Awkward column names
Backticks everywhere: `Height_1(cm)`
janitor::clean_names()


Dates read as text
bronc_date is <chr>
Use read_csv(), or parse with lubridate


Duplicate IDs
Row counts grow after a join

Permission or lock errors on Windows

Bring a pandas DataFrame back to R (py$ in R)

title: Using one dataset in both R and Python
text:
Why use both?
R and Python each have strengths. R has dplyr, ggplot2 and a deep set of statistics and Bioconductor packages; Python has pandas, scikit-learn and most machine learning tools. With reticulate, a single Quarto document (or R session) can run both languages and pass data between them, without saving and re-reading CSV files in between.

title: Using one dataset in both R and Python
text:
1. Set up reticulate
reticulate needs a Python installation with pandas. Using a project-specific environment keeps package versions stable. For example, with uv in your project folder:
uv init --bare
uv add pandas numpy
Then tell reticulate to use it, before any Python code runs:

library(reticulate)
use_python(here::here(".venv", "bin", "python"))   # on Windows: ".venv/Scripts/python.exe"

Check that reticulate found Python and pandas:

py_module_available("pandas")

[1] TRUE

py_version()

[1] '3.12'








Tip



Once Python has started in an R session, reticulate can’t switch to another Python. If it picked the wrong one, restart R (Session → Restart R) and call use_python() first. Setting the RETICULATE_PYTHON environment variable in your project’s .Renviron makes the choice permanent.

title: Using one dataset in both R and Python
text:
2. Prepare the data in R
Load the baseline table and the baseline-visit cell counts, as in Tutorial 1, and join them:

library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)
library(ggplot2)


missing_codes <- c("", "N/A", "ND", ".", "-", "not done")

baseline <- read_csv(baseline_path) |>
  distinct(pt_id, .keep_all = TRUE)            # two participants were entered twice

baseline_cells <- read_excel(cells_path, sheet = "Baseline", col_types = "text") |>
  type_convert(na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names() |>
  select(pt_id, macrophages_percent, lymphocytes_percent, neutrophils_percent)

bal <- baseline |>
  left_join(baseline_cells, by = "pt_id") |>
  mutate(
    tb_diagnosis = factor(tb_diagnosis, levels = c("Control", "LTBI", "Active TB")),
    viability_percent = 100 * live_cells / total_cells
  ) |>
  select(pt_id, sex, tb_diagnosis, hiv_status, age_at_visit, bronc_date,
         total_cells, viability_percent, time_to_process_min,
         macrophages_percent, lymphocytes_percent, neutrophils_percent)

title: Using one dataset in both R and Python
text:
3. From R to Python: r.
Inside a Python chunk, every object in the R session is available through r. Reading r.bal converts the R data frame to a pandas DataFrame:

import pandas as pd

Two conversions need care, because neither raises an error.

Pitfall 1: integer columns with missing values
R stores a missing integer as a special number. pandas’ standard integer type has no way to represent “missing”, so that special number comes through as if it were a real value:

demo <- data.frame(minutes = c(120L, NA, 95L))   # 120L means "integer 120"
demo

  minutes
1     120
2      NA
3      95



r.demo

      minutes
0         120
1 -2147483648
2          95


The missing value became -2147483648, and any average you calculate in Python is now wrong. Convert integer columns to doubles in R before sending them:

demo <- demo |>
  mutate(across(where(is.integer), as.double))


r.demo

   minutes
0    120.0
1      NaN
2     95.0








Tip



read_csv() and read_excel() read numbers as doubles, so you mainly meet this with columns you created with as.integer(), 1L or functions such as n().




Pitfall 2: dates
R Date columns arrive as a column of plain Python date objects (dtype object), not as pandas dates:

print(bal["bronc_date"].dtype)

object

<class 'datetime.date'>

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Why I built this
Most of my work so far has been in clinical genomics and tuberculosis research. I wanted a project that showed the same skills (messy data, careful pipelines, honest modelling) applied to a business problem, and credit risk is one of the most common uses of data science in South African banking and insurance.
The lender in this project needs to answer three questions:

Which applicants are likely to default? A model that ranks new applicants by risk at the point of application.
Where is the portfolio risk concentrated? Default rates by province, channel and time.
Which marketing campaigns are worth the money? Cost per application and cost per approved loan.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Architecture






flowchart LR
    A[Source files] --> B[Bronze<br/>raw + lineage]
    B --> C[Silver<br/>cleaned and validated]
    C --> D[Gold<br/>model-ready tables]
    D --> E[Models<br/>MLflow]
    D --> F[Dashboard and<br/>risk report]
    E --> F













Layer
What happens




Bronze
Source files loaded as-is, with lineage columns recording the source file, sheet and ingestion time


Silver
IDs standardised, money, numbers and dates parsed, categories mapped, out-of-range values nulled, duplicates removed, quality checks enforced


Gold
One row per loan with application-time features and a default label, plus campaign attribution and efficiency tables


Model
Time-based train/test split, two models compared, metrics and models logged to MLflow



One notebook, 00_run_all, runs every stage in order and prints a summary of the gold table and the latest model results.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Cleaning messy data
The source data has the kinds of problems real lending data has. Rather than fixing them ad hoc, I wrote shared functions in src/cleaning.py that every notebook uses.







Problem in the source
How the pipeline handles it




IDs written as c00042, C 0042, 42
Standardised to C00042


Money as R 7350, R7,350, 7350.00
Currency symbols, spaces and commas stripped


Dates in seven formats, some with two-digit years
Each format tried in turn; dates outside a valid range rejected


Null markers such as N/A, ND, unknown, -
Recognised by one shared pattern and treated as missing


Free-text categories (gau, Gauteng, GAUTENG)
Mapped to standard values; ambiguous ones (Nor) reported and left blank rather than guessed


Campaigns with swapped dates or negative spend
Corrected and flagged



For example, a single function handles every money format:
def parse_money(df, c):
    """'R 7350', 'R7,350', '7350.00' -> 7350.0"""
    t = F.regexp_replace(F.trim(F.col(c)), r"[Rr,\s]", "")
    return df.withColumn(
        c,
        F.when(F.col(c).rlike(NULL_TOKENS), F.lit(None).cast("double"))
         .otherwise(t.try_cast("double")),
    )
Every silver table must also pass checks before it is written: unique keys, no unparsed dates, and no orphaned records (for example, repayments for a loan that does not exist). If a check fails, the pipeline stops, so bad data never reaches the gold layer.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Building a leakage-free loan table
The gold layer is where most of the modelling decisions live. Three of them matter most.
1. Only use what was known at application time. For example, the number of previous applications counts only those made before the current one:
w = (Window.partitionBy("customer_id")
     .orderBy("application_date", "application_id")
     .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, -1))
apps = apps.withColumn("n_prior_applications", F.count("*").over(w))
2. A clear definition of default. A loan counts as defaulted if it reaches 90+ days past due within its first 6 instalments, or within the full term for shorter loans.
3. Only label loans that have been watched long enough. A loan that has defaulted after three months is easy to label, but a loan that is three months old and still paying might default next month. Labelling it “no default” too early would make recent loans look safer than they are. So loans that have not been observed for the full window get no label:
defaulted = F.col("max_dpd") >= 90
matured = F.col("n_observed") >= window_len

g = (g.withColumn("matured", F.coalesce(matured, F.lit(False)))
      .withColumn("default_flag", F.when(F.col("matured"), defaulted.cast("int"))))
This leaves 6,276 matured loans with a 19.7% default rate for modelling, out of 9,564 in total.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Modelling
I split the data by time: the model trains on the oldest 80% of loans and is tested on the newest 20%. That is how a lender would actually use it, trained on past customers and applied to future ones. A random split would let the model learn from loans that came after the ones it is tested on.
I compared two models inside the same scikit-learn pipeline (median imputation, scaling and one-hot encoding), with every run logged to MLflow:



Model
Test AUC
Test Gini




Logistic regression
0.668
0.336


Gradient boosting
0.626
0.253



Logistic regression won. With around 5,000 training loans, gradient boosting overfits slightly, while the simpler model generalises better to new loans. Lenders also tend to prefer logistic regression, because each feature’s effect can be explained to regulators and credit committees.
Features used: loan terms (principal, term, interest rate), affordability (income, debt-to-income, loan-to-income), credit history (bureau score, no-bureau-hit flag, prior applications), applicant details (age, employment duration, employer type, province) and channel type.






TipA deliberate exclusion



Sex is in the data but not in the model. South Africa’s National Credit Act prohibits unfair discrimination in credit decisions, and a production scorecard would not use it.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Dashboard
The dashboard is built in Databricks AI/BI on the gold tables and gives a credit manager a one-page view of the portfolio.



Portfolio overview: applications, loans disbursed, principal lent, default rate, approval decisions and the monthly disbursement trend.





Loans brought in by each marketing campaign.





Default rate by province.





Borrower profile by province: bureau score, income, debt-to-income and default rate.





Loan volume by partner channel.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
What I learned

Most of the work is in the data, not the model. Cleaning six messy tables and getting the label right took far longer than training, and mattered more for the result.
Data leakage hides in ordinary-looking choices. Using a random split, or labelling recent loans as non-defaulters, would both have produced a better-looking score that would not hold up in practice.
Simpler can be better. The more complex model scored lower on future loans.
Shared, tested functions pay off. Writing the cleaning and quality checks once and reusing them made the pipeline easier to debug and rerun.

Next steps

Improve the features, compare a binned (weight-of-evidence) scorecard, and tune hyperparameters
Check calibration, so predicted default probabilities match observed default rates
Schedule the pipeline as a Databricks job, with monitoring for data drift and model performance

TipLooking back (November 2026)



This was one of my first portfolio analyses, written in February 2026. If I did it again, I would calculate the key takeaways directly from the data rather than typing them in, and use Welch’s t-test, which doesn’t assume the two groups have equal variances. I would also fit a logistic regression so that age, sex and ventilation are considered together: ventilated patients were probably sicker to begin with, so comparing them directly overstates ventilation’s link with mortality. With 103 patients from one hospital, I would frame the findings more cautiously too. My credit risk pipeline shows how my approach has changed since.

title: COVID-19 Blood Counts and Patient Outcomes
text:
Introduction:
Coronavirus Disease 2019 (Covid-19) is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which emerged as a global pandemic in early 2020. It primarily spreads through respiratory particles and has impacted global health, economics and societies worldwide.

Project Context and Motivation:
This Quarto document serves as an exercise in Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), focusing on a critical public health data-set related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The data, sourced from a collaborative research effort, provides clinical insights into patient outcomes based on complete blood count (CBC) metrics (Rahman et al., 2020) .


Data Source and Collection Methodology:
The data-set was compiled by a team of researchers and medical professionals from Qatar University and Dhaka Medical College Hospital, Bangladesh. Data collection occurred between April 12 and August 31, 2020, at the Dhaka Medical College Hospital, following approval from the local Hospital Ethical Committee. This specific time frame places the data collection during a significant early phase of the pandemic (Rahman et al., 2020).

title: COVID-19 Blood Counts and Patient Outcomes
text:
Import modules & packages:
Analysis was conducted primarily using Python, leveraging key libraries from the scientific Python ecosystem: pandas (team, 2020), Numpy (Harris et al., 2020), Seaborn (Waskom, 2021), Matplotlib (Hunter, 2007), and SciPy (Virtanen et al., 2020).
For alternative R analysis, the comprehensive tidyverse package was loaded (Wickham et al., 2019).

import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
sns.set()

title: COVID-19 Blood Counts and Patient Outcomes
text:
Demographic Distributions:

Patient Age Distribution:








Figure 1: Histogram showing the distribution of patient ages within the dataset.





Figure 1 reveals a multimodal age distribution with peaks around 30-40, 50-60, and 60-70 years, spanning 17, 77 years overall. This middle-aged concentration reflects hospital admission patterns during early pandemic waves. Central tendency centers around 46 years with moderate spread (SD \(\pm\) 16)


Gender Composition:








Figure 2: Gender Distribution





Nearly balanced gender representation, 55 males, 48 females) minimizes sampling bias, as shown in Figure 2. This equilibrium supports gender-stratified analyses without confounding by disproportionate representation.


Survival Pattern Analysis:

Age-Survival Relationship:








Figure 3: Age Survival Relationship





Violin plots, Figure 3, demonstrates clear age-outcome divergences: recovered patients peak at 30-50 years while non-recovered concentrate above 60 years. Survival rates decline sharply: 87%, < 40 years, 57%, 40-60 years, and 24%, > 60 years.

|:------------|--------------:|------------------:|----:|

| >60         |          24.1 |              75.9 |  29 |







Clinical Outcomes by Gender:

Figure 4 shows proportional recovery rates (\(\pm\) 59% overall) identical across genders despite higher raw non-recovery counts among males.



Clinical Trajectory Metrics:

Hospital Length Stay:
Length of Stay (LOS), Figure 5, reveal shorter median stays for recovered patients versus prolonged stays for non-recovered cases, reflecting disease severity.








Figure 5: Length of Stay







Ventilation and Treatment Analysis:



Table 4: Ventilation and treatment analysis



| Ventilated (Y/N)   |   Not Recovered |   Recovered |

Ventilated patients showed a 70% mortality rate vs 35% mortality rate for the non-ventilated patients.


Clinical Variable Intercorrelations:








Figure 6: Correlation Heatmap





The expanded heatmap, Figure 6, highlights strongest relationships: neutrophils - lymphocytes. Notable absent: age-outcome correlation due to categorical target encoding. Weak age associations with blood metrics suggest independent demographic effects.



Statistical Hypothesis Testing:


Gender-Survival Chi-square: χ²=2.68, p=0.1016


Age by Outcome T-test: t=-6.90, p=0.0000



Chi-square test for gender-survival association:
A Chi-square test of independence was performed to examine the relationship between patient gender and survival outcome.
The analysis produced \(x^2\) statistic of 2.68 with a corresponding p-value of 0.1016. Since the p-value is greater than the standard significance level of 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, that gender and survival are independent.
The statistical evidence suggests there is no significant association between a patient’s gender and their likelihood of recovery within this specific data-set. This supports the visual observation from Figure 2 , indicating similar proportional outcomes for both males and females.


T-Test for age difference by outcome:
An independent samples T-test was conducted to compare the mean age of patients who recovered versus those who did not recover.
The T-test yielded a T-statistic of -6.90 and an extremely low p-value. As the p-value is well below the 0.05 significance threshold, we reject the null hypothesis.
The negative T-statistic indicates that patients who recovered were, on average, younger than those who did not recover. This provides support for Figure 3 , highlighting age as a critical predictor of outcome in this cohort.

text:
Key Takeaways:


1. Age >60 years: 76% mortality risk (t=-6.90, p<0.0001, d=1.4)


2. No missing data - excellent quality


3. Multimodal age distribution (peaks: 30-40, 50-60, 60-70)


4. Gender not significant predictor


5. Ventilation: 70% case fatality rate vs 35% non-ventilated

I would also describe the correlations as associations rather than “drivers”, and check the findings against the official WHO Global TB Report data before drawing conclusions. title: Global Tuberculosis Trends, 2000–2024
text:
Introduction:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant global health challenge, affecting millions of people worldwide, particularly in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. The World Health Organization (WHO) adopted a blueprint in 2014, the End TB Strategy, which aims to reduce incidence by 80% by the year 2030, using the year 2015 as a baseline.
This project conducts an exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the Tuberculosis_Trends.csv (Kyada, 2024) dataset available on Kaggle, which captures comprehensive country-level public health data from 2000 - 2024. The primary objective is to uncover patterns and relationships between TB indicators (cases, mortality, treatment success) and various socio-economic and health infrastructure metrics to identify key drivers of disease prevalence. Specifically, this analysis aims to answer:

How have TB cases and deaths trended in South Africa compared to other regions?
What socio-economic or health infrastructure factors show the strongest correlation with reduced TB burden?
Does the current trajectory indicate South Africa will meet the 2030 reduction targets?

Conclusion and Actionable Recommendations:
This exploratory data analysis and predictive modeling project successfully identified key drivers of tuberculosis prevalence in South Africa and forecasted potential future trends. The analysis highlights that South Africa, under its current trajectory, is not projected to meet the ambitious 80% TB incidence reduction target by 2030.
Key Takeaways and Insights:

The strongest negative correlation was found between Access_To_Health_Services and TB_Deaths.
GDP_Per_Capita and TB_Treatment_Success_Rate were significant features in predicting TB cases, along with general population density.
The high variability of HIV co-infected cases highlights a need for better integrated screening and treatment programs.

Next Steps:
Future work will involve validating the insights found here by analyzing the official WHO Global TB Report dataset, as the current analysis utilizes a similar but separate dataset obtained via Kaggle. Additionally, future analysis could incorporate more granular geographic data to identify specific TB hotspots, perform cost-effectiveness analysis for the recommended interventions, or explore more advanced time-series models to refine long-term forecasting.
Limitations:

The analysis utilized a dataset obtained via Kaggle, which is similar to but separate from the official WHO Global TB Report dataset. Future work would involve validating these insights against the official WHO data.
The correlation analysis and predictive modeling were specifically conducted using data only for South Africa, limiting the immediate generalizability of these specific findings to other countries or regions.
Official death counts can be complex due to reporting issues (e.g., HIV and TB are often under-reported on death certificates), which may introduce some bias into the historical data.
While a Random Forest Regressor was used, future analysis could explore more advanced time-series models to refine long-term forecasting accuracy.

text: This analysis evaluates transcriptional variations on Chromosome X (chrX) between male and female individuals to uncover sex-specific dynamics. This study utilizes a cohort of 12 paired-end RNA Sequencing (RNAseq) samples obtained from distinct geographical populations. By adjusting for population structure, this analysis isolates robust sex-linked genetic expression underlying chromosome-wide regulation mechanisms.

Differential Expression
Downstream Differential Expression (DE) modeling was performed at the gene level using the Ballgown R package. To isolate sexual differences, phenotypic sex was treated as the primary covariate. Population origin was strictly embedded as a confounding adjustment variable to account for ancestry-driven batch effects. Statistical significance was controlled using False Discovery Rate (FDR) threshold of \(q-value < 0.05\).

Results

Transcript Filtering
An initial set of 2,343 transcripts was extracted from the StringTie quantification step. To eliminate uninformative background noise and improve statistical power, transcripts with low variance across samples were pruned. Applying a filtration cutoff threshold of \(rowVar > 1\) successfully yielded 1,095 high-confidence transcripts retained for exploratory and differential expression processing.


Exploratory Variance Analysis
To understand global relationship structures within the filtered datasets, a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was calculated on transcript-level Fragments Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads (FPKM) expression data.
As plotted in Figure 1, the first two principal components explained 27.1% of total variance (PC1: 14.4%, PC2: 12.7%). The distribution patterns reveal a modest separation based on biological sex along the axis trajectories. Concurrently, clear macro-clusters demonstrate underlying population structure, showing distinct spatial partitioning between European (GBR) and African (YRI) cohorts. This population grouping confirms the necessity of utilizing nested model adjustments within the F-test framework to avoid ancestry-driven false-positive discoveries.

Statistical testing on the curated genomic features revealed a highly localized set of differentially expressed targets. As mapped out in Figure 2, only three specific genes crossed the designated horizontal significance threshold of \(q = 0.05\). Fold-change computations reflect expression levels of males relative to females; consequently, negative log2 fold-change parameters pinpoint strong female-biased gene expression patterns.
The three significant genes identified are:

XIST (MSTRG.332): Shows an extreme female bias with a fold change value of 0.00229 and a significance score (\(q = 5.3 \times 10^{-7}\)).
TSIX (MSTRG.331): Displays an aligned female bias with an intermediate fold change metric of 0.01181 (\(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-6}\)).
KDM6A (MSTRG.233): Reaches significant separation parameters with an adjusted fold change value of 0.57437 (\(q = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\)).



Gene Abundance Quantification
To validate individual candidate patterns, expression profiles were plotted using log2 (FPKM + 1) metrics. The resulting boxplots (Figure 3) illustrate clear group distributions:

XIST and TSIX Expression: Both features exhibit definitive binary regulation profiles. Abundance levels are highly elevated in females (with median log2 values resting between 6.0 and 9.0) but drop down to zero baseline noise across all male samples. This is consistent with their known roles: XIST drives female-specific X-Chromosome Inactivation (XCI), while TSIX acts as its antisense regulator partner.
KDM6A Expression: Unlike the regulatory Ribonucleic acid (RNA), KDM6A is actively transcribed in both sexes. However, female samples present a statistically elevated expression ceiling compared to male profiles. This matches its classification as an XCI-escape gene that regularly maintains dual-dosage activity in female tissue.

title: Differential Expression Analysis of Chromosome X RNA-seq Data
text:
Discussion and Conclusion

Biological Implications of Female-Biased Expression
The differential expression analysis of human Chromosome X transcripts revealed a highly localized regulatory signature. Only three genes - XIST, TSIX, and KDM6A - exhibited statistically significant expression differences between sexes (\(q < 0.05\)). All three candidates demonstrated explicit female-biased abundance. This tight localization underscores the stringent evolutionary conservation governing sex-chromosome dosage mechanisms in humans.


Mechanistic Synergy of XIST and TSIX
The identification of XIST (MSTRG.332) and TSIX (MSTRG.331) as the most statistically significant differentially expressed features aligns with established models of XCI (Lyon, 1961; Galupa and Heard, 2018). In female mammals, dosage compensation between XX and XY individuals is achieved by transcriptionally silencing one of the two female X chromosomes.

XIST Function: This long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) is transcribed exclusively from the future inactive X chromosome (\(X_i\)). It physically coats the chromosome in cis, recruiting repressive chromatin-modifying complexes to initiate heterochromatin silencing.
TSIX Function: Operating as an antisense lncRNA partner, TSIX is transcribed from the opposite strand (Lee and Lu, 1999) and overlaps the XIST locus. It acts as a negative regulator of XIST. Prior to inactivation, TSIX expression on the future active X chromosome (\(X_a\)) represses XIST accumulation, preserving transcription.

The binary expression profiles captured in the FPKM boxplots (Figure 3) — where both lncRNAs show near-zero baseline expression across all male samples — reflect this strict functional biology. Because males possess only a single, active X chromosome, the XIST/TSIX inactivation locus is never activated.


Dosage Escape by KDM6A
The significant female bias observed in KDM6A (MSTRG.233) highlights a distinct biological phenomenon: XCI escape. KDM6A encodes a histone demethylase responsible for removing repressive H3K27me3 marks, thereby promoting transcriptionally active chromatin states.
Unlike XIST and TSIX, KDM6A maintains active transcription in male individuals. However, its elevated expression in females confirms that it escapes complete epigenetic silencing (Balaton, Cotton and Brown, 2015) on the inactive X chromosome. Because KDM6A is transcribed from both the active and inactive X chromosomes in females, it avoids single-dosage constraint, resulting in a higher steady-state messenger RNA (mRNA) abundance relative to males. This dual-dosage profile may contribute to sex-specific differences in immune responses and oncogenic susceptibility, as KDM6A plays a key role in chromatin remodeling.


Conclusion
By controlling for confounding population structures via Ballgown’s nested F-test framework, this study isolated true sex-linked transcriptional signals from geographic background noise. The identification of XIST, TSIX, and KDM6A validates the RNAseq processing pipeline, as these targets represent the canonical core of human X-chromosome regulation. The clear separation of population cohorts in the exploratory PCA highlights the necessity of accounting for genetic ancestry in multi-population expression studies to prevent false-positive discoveries.

title: Compartmental TB Diagnostics: A Simulated BAL Cytokine Cohort
text:
Analytical and Clinical Objective
The primary objective of this project is to build and evaluate a 3-class machine learning classifier (Active TB vs. Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) vs. Uninfected) using the multiplex cytokine panel. Model performance will be bench-marked directly against the World Health Organization (WHO) Target Product Profile (TPP) for a TB triage test, which requires a minimum acceptable performance threshold of \(≥90%\) sensitivity and \(≥70\%\) specificity.

title: Compartmental TB Diagnostics: A Simulated BAL Cytokine Cohort
text:
Library import
This project implements a multilingual data science workflow, utilizing R for data engineering and statistical analysis, and Python for predictive modeling. Data ingestion, programmatic cleaning, and parsing are executed using the R tidyverse core ecosystem, specifically dplyr (Wickham et al., 2026), tidyr (Wickham, Vaughan and Girlich, 2026), stringr (Wickham, 2025), and janitor (Firke, 2024). Descriptive clinical tables and baseline group statistics are compiled using the R packages gtsummary (Sjoberg et al., 2021) and broom (Robinson et al., n.d.), while exploratory data visualization and dimensional reduction are conducted via ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016) and factoextra (Kassambara and Mundt, 2026).
If the analytical scope expands to predictive modeling, the workflow transitions to Python via the reticulate (Ushey, Allaire and Tang, 2025) interface. This pipeline leverages Python’s machine learning libraries, including scikit-learn for cross-validation and evaluation metrics, xgboost for gradient-boosted decision tree architecture, and shap for model feature attribution.

title: Using R and Python Together in Data Science
text:
TipLooking back (November 2026)



I wrote this in February 2026, early in learning to combine R and Python. Looking back, I scaled the data before splitting it into training and test sets, which lets information from the test set leak into training; scaling inside a scikit-learn Pipeline avoids that. With only 64 samples, a single 70/30 split also gives an unstable accuracy estimate, so cross-validation would be more reliable. And with over 22,000 genes, comparisons between groups need correcting for multiple testing. My second tutorial covers passing data between R and Python more carefully.

title: Using R and Python Together in Data Science
text:
Introduction:
The age old debate, which is better, R or Python? The answer is, it depends. Both languages have their strengths and weaknesses, and the best choice for a data scientist will depend on their specific needs and preferences. In this tutorial, we will explore the use of R and Python in data science.
In bioinformatics, we frequently encounter the ‘Curse of Dimensionality’ (the (pn) problem). Here, our dataset contains over 22,000 gene features but only 64 biological samples. Navigating this requires a bilingual approach: using Python’s scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) for efficient dimensionality reduction and R’s gtsummary (Sjoberg et al., 2021) for rigorous statistical validation.

Importing libraries, Modules and data:
The first library that needs to be imported, reticulate (Ushey, Allaire and Tang, 2025), is an R package that provides an interface to Python. It allows you to run Python code from R and to use Python libraries in R. The second library, tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019), is a collection of R packages that are designed for data science. It includes packages for data manipulation, visualization, and modeling.
The python modules that need to be imported are pandas (team, 2020), numpy(Harris et al., 2020), matplotlib.pyplot(Hunter, 2007), and seaborn (Waskom, 2021). Pandas (team, 2020) is a library for data manipulation and analysis. It provides data structures and functions for working with structured data. Numpy (Harris et al., 2020) is a library for numerical computing. It provides functions for working with arrays and matrices. Matplotlib.pyplot (Hunter, 2007) is a library for creating static, animated, and interactive visualizations in Python. Seaborn (Waskom, 2021) is a library for making statistical graphics in Python. It is built on top of matplotlib (Hunter, 2007) and provides a high-level interface for drawing attractive and informative statistical graphics.

# Importing libraries
library(reticulate)
library(tidyverse)
library(ivo.table)
library(gtsummary)


# Importing modules
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import kagglehub
import os
from kagglehub import KaggleDatasetAdapter
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report



Import data from kaggle:
Data can be imported from Kaggle using the kagglehub library. The dataset_load() function is used to load a specific file from a Kaggle dataset. The handle of the dataset and the path to the specific file need to be provided as arguments to the function. This method avoids the DeprecationWarning that occurs when using the kaggle library directly.
The ‘magic’ of this workflow lies in the reticulate package (Ushey, Allaire and Tang, 2025). When we load data in a Python chunk, it is stored in the Python memory space. We can then access that exact same data in an R chunk using the py$ prefix (e.g., py$df). This allows for a seamless handover from data processing to statistical reporting without the need to export and re-import CSV files.

Data Availability & Attribution:
This analysis utilizes the Leukemia gene expression dataset from the Curated Microarray Database (CuMiDa). The data was accessed via Kaggle. This dataset is provided under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International license.


Python Kaggle Data Loading Code
# 1. Handle name: "user/dataset-slug"
handle = "brunogrisci/leukemia-gene-expression-cumida"
# 2. Specific file: ensure it matches the dataset's content
file_path = "Leukemia_GSE9476.csv"

# Use dataset_load() to avoid the DeprecationWarning
df = kagglehub.dataset_load(
    KaggleDatasetAdapter.PANDAS,
    handle=handle,
    path=file_path
)

rows = len(df)
columns = f'{len(df.columns):,}'

print(f"Data loaded successfully! Shape: {df.shape}")


Data loaded successfully! Shape: (64, 22285)


The dataset contains 64 samples and 22,285 columns, with the second column being the type of leukemia and the remaining columns representing gene expression levels. The dataset can be explored using the head() function to view the first few rows of the data.



Principal Component Analysis (PCA):
Before building a predictive model, we use Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to project these 22,000+ dimensions into 2D space. This helps us visualize whether the leukemia subtypes—such as AML versus Bone Marrow samples—naturally cluster together. If we see clear separation in the PCA plot, it provides biological confidence that a machine learning classifier will be successful.


Variance explained by top 2 components: 34.22%

  geom_point(size = 3, alpha =  0.7) +
  labs(title = "PCA of Leukemia Gene Expression Data",

  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Set1')









The PCA plot shows the distribution of samples based on the first two principal components. Different colors represent different types of leukemia, allowing for visual assessment of how well the types are separated in the reduced dimensional space. I used reticulate to leverage Python’s robust data manipulation and machine learning libraries while utilizing R’s powerful visualization capabilities to create the PCA plot. This combination allows for efficient data processing and insightful visual representation of the results.

NoteAt a glance




What: a modular Nextflow DSL2 pipeline that turns raw paired-end whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reads into a joint-called, quality-filtered set of variants

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
Why I built it
My honours project compared variant calls made against the standard human reference genome, GRCh38 (Schneider et al., 2017), with calls made against a population-specific reference genome.
That comparison set three requirements:

Reproducible: every sample goes through exactly the same steps, with the same tools and settings.
Reference-agnostic: the same pipeline runs against either reference with a single switch, keeping the outputs apart.
HPC-friendly: whole genomes produce very large intermediate files, so the pipeline has to fit a shared cluster’s storage, memory and wall-time limits.

Nextflow (Di Tommaso et al., 2017) fits all three: each step is an isolated process, runs are resumable, and the same code can run on a laptop or a PBS cluster.

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
How it works






flowchart LR
    A[Paired-end<br/>FASTQ] --> B[Align<br/>BWA-MEM]
    B --> C[SAM → BAM<br/>sort, index<br/>SAMtools]
    C --> D[Base quality<br/>recalibration<br/>GATK BQSR]
    D --> E[Per-sample<br/>GVCF<br/>HaplotypeCaller]
    E --> F[Joint genotyping<br/>GenomicsDBImport<br/>GenotypeGVCFs]
    F --> G[Variant filtering<br/>VQSR<br/>SNPs + indels]
    G --> H[Filtered<br/>cohort VCF]






Read quality was checked with FastQC (Andrews, 2010) and summarised across samples with MultiQC (Ewels et al., 2016) before reads entered the pipeline. The pipeline then follows GATK’s best-practice workflow for germline short variants (Van der Auwera and O’Connor, 2020):








Step
Tool (version)
What it does




Align
BWA-MEM 0.7.7 (Li and Durbin, 2009; Li, 2013)
Maps each sample’s read pairs to the chosen reference, adding a read group (sample, library, MGI platform) that GATK needs downstream


Convert, sort, index
SAMtools 1.9 (Danecek et al., 2021)
Converts the text SAM output to compressed BAM, sorts reads by position and indexes them


Recalibrate base qualities
GATK 4.6 BaseRecalibrator and ApplyBQSR (McKenna et al., 2010; DePristo et al., 2011)
Corrects systematic errors in the sequencer’s base quality scores, using dbSNP (Sherry, Ward and Sirotkin, 1999) as known variant sites


Call variants per sample
GATK 4.6 HaplotypeCaller, GVCF mode (Poplin et al., 2017)
Calls variants by local re-assembly and records every position, so samples can be genotyped together later


Joint genotyping
GATK 4.6 GenomicsDBImport and GenotypeGVCFs (Poplin et al., 2017)
Combines all samples’ GVCFs, chromosome by chromosome (1–22, X, Y), and genotypes them as one cohort


Filter variants
GATK 4.2.6 VariantRecalibrator and ApplyVQSR (DePristo et al., 2011)
Learns what true variants look like from trusted resources and filters the rest at 99% truth sensitivity, with separate models for SNPs and indels



The variant filtering step trains on well-established resources: HapMap 3.3 (International HapMap 3 Consortium, 2010) and the 1000 Genomes Omni 2.5 genotypes (The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2015) for SNPs, the Mills and 1000 Genomes gold-standard indels (Mills et al., 2011) for indels, and dbSNP (Sherry, Ward and Sirotkin, 1999) as known sites. The filtered SNPs and indels are then merged into a single indexed cohort VCF.

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
Engineering details

One module per step
Each step is a separate DSL2 module (modules/local/<step>/main.nf), and the main workflow only wires them together. That keeps each step small, testable and easy to swap out:


script.nf (excerpt)

workflow {
    aligned_sams = ALIGN(samples_ch, reference_ch)
    aligned_bams = SAM_TO_BAM(aligned_sams)
    sorted_bams  = SORT_BAM(aligned_bams)
    indexed_bams = INDEX_BAM(sorted_bams.sorted_bam)

    bqsr_bams = BQSR(indexed_bams, reference_ch, reference_index_ch,
                     reference_dict_ch, dbsnp_ch, dbsnp_index_ch)

    gvcfs = HAPLOTYPECALLER(bqsr_bams, reference_ch,
                            reference_index_ch, reference_dict_ch)
    // ... joint genotyping and variant filtering
}



One switch for the reference genome
A single parameter chooses the reference. Outputs are named and stored separately per reference, so a GRCh38 run and a population-reference run never overwrite each other:


modules/local/haplotypecaller/main.nf (excerpt)

publishDir "${params.outdir}/haplotypecaller/${params.use_sac_ref ? 'sac' : 'grch38'}",
           mode: 'symlink'



Dry runs without data
Every module has a stub: block that creates empty placeholder outputs. Running nextflow run script.nf -stub checks that all the channels connect correctly in seconds, without real data and without using cluster time:


modules/local/bqsr/main.nf (excerpt)

stub:
"""
touch ${sampleId}.recal.bam
touch ${sampleId}.recal.bai
"""



Fitting a shared cluster

Storage: an aligned whole genome in SAM format can be tens of gigabytes. Intermediate outputs are published as symbolic links (mode: 'symlink') rather than copies, and only the final filtered VCF is copied.
Resources: memory and CPUs are set per process, so heavy steps such as alignment get what they need without over-allocating light ones.
Software: each process loads its own pinned tool version through the cluster’s environment modules.



nextflow.config (excerpt, cluster details replaced)

process {
    queue          = 'normal'
    clusterOptions = '-P <project-code>'

    withName: 'ALIGN' {
        beforeScript = 'module load BWA/0.7.7'
        memory = '38 GB'
    }
    withName: 'HAPLOTYPECALLER' {
        beforeScript = 'module load gatk/4.6.0.0'
        memory = '8 GB'
        cpus   = 5
    }
}



Joint calling that scales
Calling each sample to a GVCF first, then genotyping the cohort together, means that adding samples later only needs the new samples to be called. It also improves genotype accuracy at sites with low coverage in some samples (Poplin et al., 2017).

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
What I’d do differently
Looking back, these are the changes I would make:

Mark duplicates before recalibration. GATK’s best practices include MarkDuplicates between alignment and BQSR (Van der Auwera and O’Connor, 2020); the pipeline goes straight from sorting to BQSR.
Stream instead of writing SAM files. Piping bwa mem directly into samtools sort would skip the large intermediate SAM files entirely.
Make quality control part of the pipeline. FastQC and MultiQC were configured but run separately; wiring them in would make each run fully self-contained.
Use containers and profiles. Docker or Singularity containers and Nextflow configuration profiles, instead of cluster-specific modules and paths, would let the pipeline run unchanged on any system.
Use one GATK version throughout. Variant filtering ran on GATK 4.2.6 while the other GATK steps used 4.6.
Compare references against a truth set. Counting shared and unique variants between two references shows that the call sets differ, but not which is more accurate: a reference that already contains a population’s common alleles will report fewer variants at those sites by design. A fair comparison needs a truth set, such as array genotypes for the same samples.
